title: Decode Ways
summary: Given a string of digits, determine the number of ways to decode it according to the following mapping: "1" -> 'A' "2" -> 'B' ..
statement: Given a string of digits, determine the number of ways to decode it according to the following mapping: "1" -> 'A' "2" -> 'B' ... "25" -> 'Y' "26" -> 'Z' Note that some digits can form valid codes within other codes, leading to multiple decoding possibilities. For example, the string "11106" can be decoded as: "AAJF" with the grouping (1, 1, 10, 6) "KJF" with the grouping (11, 10, 6) However, the grouping (1, 11, 06) is invalid because "06" is not a valid code (only "6" is valid). If the entire string cannot be decoded in any valid way, return 0. The test cases are generated such that the result will fit within a 32-bit integer.
constraints: 1–100 decimal digits; leading zeros are possible.
Valid codes are decimal strings 1 through 26, with no leading zero. Return the count of full-string decodings; the answer fits signed 32-bit.
hints: The final decoded letter consumes either one digit or two digits.
Add the count for each valid last segment, retaining only the preceding two prefix counts.
A nonzero last digit adds ways[i-1]; a pair between 10 and 26 adds ways[i-2]. Otherwise that contribution is zero.
A zero is usable only as part of 10 or 20. A memoized recursive suffix formulation uses the same choices.
editorial: For each prefix, count the decodings ending with a valid one-digit code and those ending with a valid two-digit code. These groups are disjoint. Keep the previous two counts rather than an entire DP table. Initialize the empty-prefix count to one and the first-digit count according to whether it is nonzero. The oracle independently enumerates all positions of cuts and validates every resulting segment.

tests.explanation: Decode as 1|2 (AB) or 12 (L), giving two ways.
The valid segmentations are 1|1|10|6 and 11|10|6. A segment 06 is invalid.
